articles.title: AI made self-hosting fun again
articles.content: I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit. I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me. Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that. Less friction Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project. Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort. In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me. Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality. Trying things I always found interesting There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them. NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server. For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time). Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week. AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations. Automating almost everything Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure. A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configurati

articles.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
articles.content: For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year . But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it. Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post. The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten ( BestBuy 20TB listing ). What a terabyte cost me Nov 2018 (10TB), $18.00 per TB; Oct 2020 (12TB), $14.58 per TB; Nov 2021 (14TB), $14.29 per TB; May 2022 (14TB), $17.86 per TB; Aug 2022 (14TB), $17.14 per TB; Oct 2023 (18TB), $11.11 per TB; Nov 2024 (20TB), $12.50 per TB; May 2025 (20TB), $14.00 per TB; Nov 2026 (20TB), $27.50 per TB What a terabyte cost me $0 $10 $20 $30 2018 2020 2022 2024 2026 Nov 2018 (10TB) · $18.00/TB Oct 2020 (12TB) · $14.58/TB Nov 2021 (14TB) · $14.29/TB May 2022 (14TB) · $17.86/TB Aug 2022 (14TB) · $17.14/TB Oct 2023 (18TB) · $11.11/TB Nov 2024 (20TB) · $12.50/TB May 2025 (20TB) · $14.00/TB Nov 2026 (20TB) · $27.50/TB $18.00 (10TB) $11.11 (18TB) $27.50 (20TB) Price per TB before tax. Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not. I dug through my receipts In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. articles.title: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad
articles.content: Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan. Image Kamil Khan Mumtaz with a British friend during his studies at the Architectural Association in London in the early 1960s. Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’ The Works in Progress Newsletter Get new articles from Works in Progress delivered to your inbox. Lahore was one of the capitals of the Mughal Empire, and has a vast endowment of historic architecture and urbanism. Mumtaz prepared a seminal report on its historic core, known as the Walled City. This photograph shows the Walled City during the colonial period. Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build new, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Image Workers’ houses at Kot Karamat, an early Mumtaz project in the lat

articles.title: YouTube Ad Punisher – Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays
articles.content: Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads. Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage. Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time. 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting. Auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed. Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time. Incognito: see the Incognito section above. Ad detected → Capture timestamp → Reload page → Auto-seek to timestamp → Resume ↓ (if 3 reloads fail) Redirect to yout-ube.com (ad-free mirror, no looping) Reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek. yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay issue that the mirror has by default. Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver) Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops ✅ Zero ads — reloads until the ad is gone (usually 1-2 cycles) ✅ Timestamp preserved — never lose your place in the video ✅ Live streams — plain reload (no timestamp to preserve) ✅ Ad history database — every ad logged with advertiser, duration, skip text, video, and timestamp ✅ Export — JSON or CSV download of all collected ad data ✅ Popup viewer — click the extension icon to see stats, top advertisers, and full history ✅ No permissions abuse — only storage and tabs , only on YouTube domains Option A — Chrome / Brave / Edge / Opera (Load unpacked) Clone the repo: git clone https://github.com/antonpictures/youtube-punisher.git Open chrome://extensions Enable Developer mode (top right) Click Load unpacked → select the youtube-punisher folder Done — activates on all YouTube pages automatically. ✅ Tested Option B — Safari (experimental: AppleScript workaround) Safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. articles.title: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' indicted for wire fraud
articles.content: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands. “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.” But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company]. The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors. The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260. The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260. articles.title: Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount
articles.content: Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us. The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the company calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”. There is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway. The Formula Take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of users. That’s it. \[C = \frac{E_{custom}}{\sqrt{U}}\] The square root is important. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a company of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged. We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient . Interpreting Your Score C < 5 Your workspace contains the default emoji set, a company logo, and :party-parrot: , which was added by someone in 2019 who has since left. Nobody uses it any more because it comes across as unprofessional . Communication is conducted exclusively via 👍. People are here for the salary, and they would like you to know that. 5 ≤ C < 20 A healthy, functional organisation. There is an emoji of the CTO’s face. It is used both supportively and as a weapon, depending on the context. 20 ≤ C < 50 Thriving. :this-is-fine: has been used over 4,000 times in #incidents . Management considers this a sign of engagement. C ≥ 50 Late-stage culture. Every variant of :thumbsup: now carries subtext. The plain default one is considered passive-aggressive. The emoji have begun to reference themselves: :old-man-yells-at-old-man: and :party-parrot-holding-a-party-parrot: . HR has requested a glossary, but no one person understands the memeology or the history of :cowboy-spongebob-on-fire-crying: . They’re afraid it might mean something rude. It does. The Participation Rate The Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was upload

articles.title: Intel One Mono font (2023)
articles.content: Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind. It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license. Identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design. Intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources. To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases . Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts. Activating the Fonts in Code Editors VSCode - In Settings, search Font Family, then specify Intel One Mono Sublime Text - Go to Sublime Text -> Preferences -> Settings and set font_face to Intel One Mono IntelliJ Platform - Go to File -> Settings -> Editor -> Font and set Font to Intel One Mono We recommend the .otf or .ttf format for desktop use. The .ttf files are also well suited for mobile apps. The .woff and .woff2 fonts are optimized for web use. Screen Rendering and Size Ranges We recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms. Available OpenType Features Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS: Programming Ligatures: To use programming ligatures, activate the ss01 feature (Stylistic Set #1). Additional refinements are available via ss02 and ss03 : Stylistic Set #2 switches the <= and >= combinations to arrow forms (math contractions being the default otherwise), and Stylistic Set #3 additionally activates a “www” ligature. Alternate three: New in release 1.5. Alternate form for three added. The round top three, numerator, denomenator, superior and inferior can be activated with stylistic Set #4. Raised Colon: The colon is automatically raised in operators, to align with math symbols. For non-programming contexts, the raised colon can be applied contextually between numbers or activated generally. The contextual option is available via ss11 (Stylistic Set #11); for the global switch use ss12 (Stylistic Set #12) or salt (Stylistic Alternates). Language Support: ccmp and locl features ensure correct display across a wide range of languages. These are usually active by default. We recommend setting the lang

articles.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
articles.content: On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers. Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available". If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on. What the rule says ​ The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence: The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model. The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account. There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas , whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms. Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change". The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory: Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects. Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data. Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product. The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it. What the MCP servers can do ​ Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner. Server What it can do What's missing compared with REST Gmail Search and read threads, create and list drafts, labels, trash, spam Send, reply, forward and editing drafts (partner-only). Filters, settings, attachment download, push notifications. Drafts with attachments are "not supported yet". articles.title: Rvoip: VoIP stack in Rust
articles.content: rvoip is a library, not a server you deploy next to your application. Signalling, media, codecs, NAT traversal, security, and the conversation model are all Rust crates in this workspace, so a call goes from your code to the wire without a separately installed SIP proxy, media server, or RTP engine. The examples below run on a laptop with nothing installed but Rust; the same crates carry the release-gated interoperability evidence against Asterisk, FreeSWITCH, Jambonz, Kamailio, and OpenSIPS. Carriers evaluating standards coverage, performance, and reliability should start with For carriers . Historical performance: published 0.5.0 One AWS c8i.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 8 cores, Intel Xeon 6, 32 GiB) running a single rvoip process, measured with the RFC 7501/7502 benchmark: Workload Max CPS CPS per vCPU Concurrent calls (10 s calls) p50 setup at 90% load p99 setup at 90% load SIP over TLS, signaling only 8,348 ~520 n/a 1 ms 6 ms SIP over UDP, signaling only 8,256 ~515 n/a 1 ms 6 ms TLS + SRTP (SDES), G.711, 10 s calls 1,124 ~70 ~11,200 1 ms 4 ms UDP + RTP, G.711, 10 s calls 1,204 ~75 ~12,000 n/m n/m At 2x capacity, rvoip keeps admitting calls at its max CPS, refuses the excess with fast 503 responses, and recovers cleanly once the load drops. Max CPS (calls per second; RFC 7502's Session Establishment Rate) is the highest rate with zero failed calls over a trial of at least 180 s and 50,000 call attempts. rvoip was measured as a terminating endpoint: it answers each call and echoes its media. A relaying B2BUA or SBC handles two call legs per session. G.711 media is passed through; nothing is transcoded. Concurrent calls is the CPS times the 10 s call length, not a measured maximum; long-call capacity, where most SBC datasheets quote their concurrency, has not been measured yet. The server is a cloud VM, not an appliance. p50 and p99 setup are the RFC 6076 session request delay measured at 90% of max CPS, recorded in whole milliseconds (so 1 ms means 1 ms or less); n/m = not measured. The UDP + RTP max CPS was confirmed twice rather than three times. The release check also passed at 5% above the TLS and UDP signaling max CPS, so those two figures may be slightly understated. Not yet measured: B2BUA/relay mode (two legs per call), registrations, transcoding, WebRTC (DTLS-SRTP), and failover. Full method and per-trial data: RFC 7501/7502 benchmark report . 1. Add one dependency. [ dependencies ] rvoip-sip = " 0.5.1 " tokio = { version = " 1 " , features = [ " full " ] } Upgrading an existing application from 0.3? The 0.4 migration guide has before/after code for every breaking change. 2. Make a call. Bob answers, Alice dials, Alice hangs up. Everything runs on loopback, so this works on a laptop with no PBX, no account, and no network setup. use std :: time :: Duration ; use rvoip_sip :: { Config , Endpoint , EndpointProfile } ; # [ tokio :: main ] async fn main ( ) -> rvoip_sip :: Result < ( ) > { let bob = tokio :: spawn ( async { let mut bob = Endpoint ::
articles.summary: rvoip 发布纯 Rust 实现的 VoIP 协议栈，集成信令、媒体、编解码与 NAT 穿透，无需独立 SIP 代理或媒体服务器。

articles.title: Slow Ubuntu security response times
articles.content: [<prev] [next>] [day] [month] [year] [list] Message-ID: <20261125172638.73c0a05b@hboeck.de> Date: Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:26:38 +0100 From: Hanno Böck <hanno@...eck.de> To: oss-security@...ts.openwall.com Subject: Slow Ubuntu security response times Hello, Lately, I'm observing that Ubuntu's response to severe security flaws is concerning. On November 16th, details about a remote memory corruption called NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) in the Linux kernel's TCP stack were published: https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/11/15/2 Today, nine days later, Ubuntu still has not published a fix yet: https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99288 Other distros had a fix already available when the details were published. Likewise, a KVM host escape (CVE-2026-99312) affecting AMD virtualization published on Nov 18th has no fix yet either [3]: https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99312 Ubuntu has been slow in patching another remote TCP corruption (CVE-2026-98432) lately, where it took multiple weeks until a fix was available. See also: https://chalmovsky.com/posts/wtf-ubuntu Recent news indicates that this is might be exploited in the wild: https://www.greynoise.io/blog/check-point-security-management-servers-intrusion-campaign I think everyone understands that these times aren't easy for security teams. Nevertheless, remote corruption vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel are the kind of thing where I expect updates to be available within hours, not days or weeks. On a recent Ubuntu LTS system, the kernel version is 7.0.0-44. This seems to indicate that Ubuntu is not relying on longterm supported kernels from kernel.org, but is instead backporting patches to an old kernel version. On a Debian stable system, the kernel version is 6.12.118+deb13, indicating that it's based on a very recent longterm kernel from kernel.org. I would consider the backporting strategy for the kernel to be hardly viable and probably everyone should base their Linux kernels on longterm releases supported by the Linux kernel developers. -- Hanno Böck - Independent security researcher https://itsec.hboeck.de/ https://badkeys.info/ Powered by blists - more mailing lists Please check out the Open Source Software Security Wiki , which is counterpart to this mailing list . Confused about mailing lists and their use? Read about mailing lists on Wikipedia and check out these guidelines on proper formatting of your messages .

articles.title: Garage v2.6.0 released with web admin, v1.x EoL & other news
articles.content: We are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-new web administration UI funded by NLnet. We also discuss many other small news: Helm chart repository release, Garage v1.x EoL, Garage v3.0.0 beta 1 and an outlook on upcoming work on S3 versioning. The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present new features and give some information on what's coming next. Garage v2.6.0 and the web administration GUI This is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander . We started this collaboration in 2024 when it was clear that a user interface was one of the most sorely lacking feature of Garage. We are very grateful that NLnet has again engaged with us and provided funding to make this a reality. Here's a minimal example to test 2.6.0 right away: cat > garage.toml <<'EOF' metadata_dir = "/var/lib/garage/meta" data_dir = "/var/lib/garage/data" db_engine = "lmdb" replication_factor = 1 rpc_bind_addr = "[::]:3901" [s3_api] s3_region = "garage" api_bind_addr = "[::]:3900" [admin] api_bind_addr = "[::]:3903" EOF TOKEN=$(openssl rand -base64 32) echo "Admin token: $TOKEN" docker run --name garage -p 3900:3900 -p 127.0.0.1:3903:3903 \ -e GARAGE_RPC_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) \ -e GARAGE_ADMIN_TOKEN="$TOKEN" \ -e GARAGE_DEFAULT_BUCKET=testbucket \ -e GARAGE_DEFAULT_ACCESS_KEY=GKthisisatestkey \ -e GARAGE_DEFAULT_SECRET_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32) \ -v $PWD/garage.toml:/etc/garage.toml:z -v garage:/var/lib/garage \ dxflrs/garage:v2.6.0 /garage server --single-node --default-bucket Running 2.6.0 or above, you can access the web interface on the garage admin API port, by default port 3903, so http://localhost:3903/ if you are running garage on your machine with the example above. Logging in requires a garage admin token. The example above prints it on the command line. If you have set the admin_token configuration variable in your configuration file, you may use that token. Otherwise, you'll need to create a separate token from the command line with garage admin-token create . One world of caution: administering a remote cluster over plain HTTP is NOT safe , as your admin token is transmitted in plain text with each request. You'll need to setup an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of your Garage node to encrypt the connection, or/and access your node through a VPN such as Wireguard to make sure no one can eavesdrop the credentials. Once logged in the cluster, you will be greeted by a cluster overview screen that looks like the following (this is a live example from our Deuxfleurs cluster): The web interface follows a similar pattern to the CLI: cluster monitoring, layout configuration, bucket and access credential management are all available as you expect. articles.title: Entering the Geminispace
articles.content: On May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread . I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that. However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/ . The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post. Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way. A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC. What is Gemini? A terrible name, that is. Looking for information about Gemini these days is extremely hard, thanks to Google polluting the namespace with its own AI offering. Of course that’s not Project Gemini’s fault because Google’s thing came after them, but still, good luck finding stuff about this network. Joking aside, let’s look at Project Gemini’s barebones front page: Project Gemini's front page, displayed in the Lagrange browser. … and break down the introductory and only paragraph: Gemini is a new internet technology supporting an electronic library of interconnected text documents. You can think of Gemini as a way to access a bunch of text-only pages, with links among them, so you can find information and follow links to additional resources. Instead of using http:// or https:// URL prefixes, you use gemini:// instead. That’s not a new idea, but it’s not old fashioned either. Exactly. Gemini is like the WWW , or “the web” in more colloquial/modern parlance. In fact, Gemini is a parallel community to the web. Obviously, that’s not a new idea because the web dates back to 1989, and we are now 37 years after that. The idea is not unique either because Gopher , a much lesser-known option, exists as well. Surprisingly to me, I realized that Gopher came after the web in 1991 while researching this article. I had always assumed Gopher was first and that the web came to replace it because of Gopher’s rigidness. But that’s not quite what happened. It’s timeless, and deserves tools which treat it as a first class concept, not a vestigial corner case. Humans have shared written documents since around 3400–3100 BCE (roughly 5,100–5,400 years ago) in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, and that’s probably (hopefully?) not going away. It’s true, though, that at this point, text sharing is not the primary thing that the web does, as you well know. We have morphed the web from a document distribution tool into an app platform, for better or

articles.title: Scott Aaronson on recent complexity theory AI achievements
articles.content: I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again. Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP —hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis , which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4 —a lower bound (!!) , matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6. There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log 2 7) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP. Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that ! But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N) 1/2+o(1) . The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log 0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!) . All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered , rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues. To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE —that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow. It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the s

articles.title: Typed indexes in Zig
articles.content: Typed indices in Zig The pattern The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays. The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me. Andrew’s example don’t show much of how to enforce the safety at call site: any caller could call @backingInt (it used to be @intFromEnum ) to recover a numerical index and pass it to the wrong array, or access array elements with a plain integer. And matklad’s one focus on building a tree data structure in a neat way, but that’s a totally different challenge that the introductory problem of mixing array indexes, so it was not a super convincing illustration for me. In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array. It can be a method on the array type—or the index type. // Declaration const Elem = struct { ... } ; const Array = struct { items : []Elem , const Index = enum ( u32 ) { _ } ; fn get ( a : *Array , i : Index ) *Elem { return &a.items[@backingInt ( i ) ] ; } } ; // Usage const a = Array { .items = &. { ... } } ; var i : Index = @fromBackingInt ( 57 ) ; _ = a.get ( i ) ; _ = a.get ( 57 ) ; // Does not compile: wrong type. _ = a[ 57 ] ; // Possible, but discouraged by the existence of `Array.get`. A struct of array example In a struct of array data structure, it is particularly valuable to have one typed index per slice rather than relying on careful naming. Consider this spreadsheet example where it’s easy to mix up indexes: pub const Sheet = struct { row_height : []f32 , col_width : []f32 , } ; var s : Sheet = . { ... } ; var r : usize = 0 ; // Row index. var c : usize = 0 ; // Column index. // User changes the column width. s.col_width[r].* = new_col_width ; // bug: access row data with a column indice! We can prevent such bug by enforcing compile time checking of field access with typed indexes. pub const Sheet = struct { row_height : []f32 , col_width : []f32 , pub const Row = enum ( u32 ) { _ } ; pub const Column = enum ( u32 ) { _ } ; pub fn getRowHeight ( s : *Sheet , r : Row ) *f32 { return &s[@backingInt ( r ) ] ; } pub fn getColWidth ( s : *Sheet , c : Column ) *f32 { return &s[@backingInt ( c ) ] ; } } ; var s : Sheet = . { ... } ; var r : Sheet.Row = @fromBackingInt ( 0 ) ; // Typed row index. var c : Sheet.Column = @fromBackingInt ( 0 ) ; // Typed column index. // User changes the column width. const new_col_width : f32 = undefined ; s.getColWidth ( r ) .* = new_col_width ; // Comptime error: wrong type. s.getColWidth ( c ) .* = new_col_width ; // Yes! s.col_width[@backingInt ( r ) ] // Possible, but very intentional. s.col_width[ 57 ] // Possible, but discouraged by // convention given by Sheet decls // and documentation. Generic recipe Its clumsy to keep one index type and one accessor per field. We can use a bit of comptime to streamline the pattern, and make the recipe more generic to fit arbitrary structs. Here is a complete example. pub const Sheet = stru

articles.title: Browser tabs as a container runtime
articles.content: tl;dr tabc is a container runtime, like runc, that runs each container in a Chromium tab. docker run --runtime tabc alpine works and starts in under a second. On a Mac it needs no hypervisor and no Linux VM ; Linux for everyone! Despite my zealot love for Nix , there is no denying the convenience and ubiquity of Docker. Containers have become the standard unit of software deployment, providing a consistent environment across different machines and simplifying the management of dependencies. 1 1 Containers are not even a “real” thing within the Linux kernel although there are recent attempts to formalize them as a kernel-level abstraction. Despite all the footguns you can get yourself into by writing a non-reproducible Dockerfile, it was a still a remarkable step forward in making software deployment more predictable and portable. Nothing has really challenged Docker’s dominance in the container space and it’s reliance on Linux as the underlying platform. The absurdity of the situation has become that developers on MacOS end up running a Linux virtual machine to simply run containers. People, even the creator of Docker, believed a common runtime for software isolation would have been a game-changer and that WebAssembly could have played that role if it had existed earlier. “If WASM+WASI existed in 2008, we wouldn’t have needed to created Docker. That’s how important it is.” - Solomon Hykes, 2019 Here we are, 7 years later, we still have Docker, and WebAssembly is mostly used for speeding up web applications. Is there another way to achieve the same level of isolation and portability without relying on the host being Linux? What if though Docker ran its containers on WebAssembly instead of directly on the Linux kernel? What if the isolation provided by the browser could replace the kernel-level isolation that containers rely on? This idea, the holy grail of running Linux in a browser is not new. JSLinux did it in 2011, and v86 , WebVM and qemu-wasm are also attempts in the same direction. They all have their share of limitations: 32-bit only, performance issues, incomplete hardware emulation, that make them impractical for general-purpose use. 1980-01-01T00:00:00+00:00 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.10.5, https://matplotlib.org/ 0.03 0.1 0.3 1 3 python3 -c 'print(1)' jj --version rg --version hello 5x 11x 13x 8x seconds, first run (log scale) a whole machine emulated only your program emulated unkernel is a newly developed project by Pooya Parsa that changes the economics of what is possible. unknernel compiles the Linux kernel to WebAssembly, allowing it to run directly in the browser without relying on traditional hardware emulation. Only your container’s own code goes through an emulator, and everything else the kernel does runs at near native speed. It is now practical to run Linux containers directly in the browser, leveraging the isolation provided by WebAssembly and the browser environment with acceptable performance. articles.title: In defense of lock poisoning in Rust (2025)
articles.content: There’s recently been some discussion about the benefits and downsides of lock (mutex) poisoning in Rust, spurred by a recent proposal to make the default mutex non-poisoned, i.e. silently unlock on panic (see also, recent discussion on Hacker News ). As a passionate defender of lock poisoning, I thought I’d gather and write about my thoughts on this matter. To summarize, I believe: Unexpected cancellations in critical sections cause real harm to system correctness. Lock poisoning is an important part of ensuring the correctness of critical sections in Rust. Poisoning applies more generally than mutexes, and providing an easy way to track that (via e.g. a Poison<T> wrapper) is valuable. While there is conceptual elegance in separating out locking from poisoning on panic, the importance of lock poisoning overrides these concerns. What is poisoning? # Rust, like most multithreaded languages, has mutexes : a construct to ensure that a particular piece of data can only be accessed by one thread at a time. The way mutexes work in Rust is particularly well-considered: Rust uses a single-ownership model, and the notion of shared ( & ) and exclusive ( &mut ) references to some data. Most data structures are written such that mutations always require a &mut reference to it. In Rust, the data guarded by a mutex is owned by the mutex. (In many other languages, you have to track the mutex and data separately, and it’s easy to get it wrong.) When you lock a mutex, you start from a shared reference: a &Mutex<T> . Once you have obtained the lock, you get back a MutexGuard<T> , which indicates that you now have exclusive access to the guarded data. The MutexGuard can give you a &mut T , so you have exclusive access to it. When the MutexGuard is dropped, the lock is released. The period during which the lock is held is called the critical section (generally, not just in Rust). This is all quite reasonable! Let’s look at an example that processes incoming messages for a set of tracked operations. Let’s assume that multiple threads could be processing messages, so we have to guard the internal state with a mutex. (We’ll discuss alternative approaches to this problem later.) A simple implementation: use std :: { collections :: HashMap , sync :: Mutex }; struct OperationId ( /* ... */ ); enum OperationState { InProgress { /* ... */ }, Completed { /* ... */ }, } impl OperationState { // Here, `process_message` consumes self and returns self. In practice this // is often because the state has some internal data that requires // processing by ownership. fn process_message ( self , message : Message ) -> Self { match self { /* ... */ } } } struct Operations { ops : Mutex < HashMap < OperationId , OperationState >> , } impl Operations { /// Process a message, updating the internal operation state appropriately. pub fn process ( & self , id : & OperationId , message : Message ) { // Obtain a lock on the HashMap. let mut lock = self . ops . lock (). unwrap (); // Once the l

articles.title: Make the Plan a Value
articles.content: Make the Plan a Value I recently finished adding support for idempotency tokens to amazonka (the unofficial Haskell AWS SDK), using the client token support provided by AWS . Implementing this required making some fairly substantial changes to the generator, the bespoke Haskell program that turns the service definitions in botocore into cabal packages. amazonka is over a decade old, and the generator has evolved as AWS have added new styles of APIs for their different services. Some services return XML, some return JSON, some return raw bytes, some return additional information in HTTP response headers, and so on. As a result, the generator’s logic had been extended each time and had grown gnarly. To untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite programming moves, “make the plan a value” or “decide what to do, and then do it”. This move decouples two parts of a program by introducing an intermediate data structure (a “plan”, or a value of a “plan type”) describing what is to be done before any action is taken. I really like this pattern because the “deciding what to do” part of a program is often more complicated than the “doing” part. Separating the two often turns the “deciding” part into a pure function that produces a plan, making test cases simpler to write. And then if the “doing” phase is also complicated (because of remote API calls, rollbacks, parallel execution, or whatever else), it’s more manageable because those complications are not entangled with the planning logic. You also get to add a --dry-run flag almost for free, which is really useful for testing . (Henrik observes that testing for a dryRun variable everywhere pollutes the code somewhat. I think if he split his code into a planning phase and consumed that plan with either a “dry run” printer or a “real” executor, the inline checks that he dislikes would disappear.) This technique isn’t subtle or obscure. I’ve seen it called the plan-execute pattern , and the “routing slip” enterprise integration pattern is literally about centralising the decision logic before execution. I’ve previously called it a “tiny DSL” , and Matt Parsons sells its benefits in his Three Layer Haskell Cake article: Often times, a simple non-recursive sum type “command” suffices as an interface between a pure function and an effectful one. A list of commands adds a lot of flexibility without dramatically complicating things. Having resolved to introduce a plan type, how do we work it into a venerable program like the Amazonka generator? For this part of the generator, it means separating the analysis of the loaded service definitions from the generation of the instance AWSRequest declarations. I did this by introducing a Config record of simple data and a function instanceD :: Config -> Decl () that builds Haskell code from that config record. I found the generator’s logic too difficult to understand and replace in a single change, so I replaced it incrementally using the strangler fig pattern

articles.title: Taking Email Back
articles.content: Three Homes, No Data Center Deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, says some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way. The software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and plans to move to Aerogramme around January 2027. The collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains. Email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence. Two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services. The Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development. articles.summary: 英国FCA投诉Meta拒绝在推出个人AI代理前共享Muse进行联合测试，警告代理攻击风险。

articles.title: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
articles.content: Ford enters the World Endurance Championship in 2027 with the new prototype.
articles.summary: 福特发布GT41原型赛车，将于2027年携新车重返世界耐力锦标赛，目标再夺勒芒冠军。

articles.title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
articles.content: Detailed estimate going back to 1800 shows how much carbon is being liberated.
articles.summary: 研究估算自1800年以来泥炭地排水释放的碳量，显示其贡献了全球变暖的百分之几。

articles.title: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
articles.content: Our home offices range from tasteful to "please explain yourself."
articles.summary: Ars员工展示各自风格迥异的家庭办公室，从极简到极繁，呈现远程办公环境多样性。

articles.title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
articles.content: "DART made a really, really large mess. However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess."
articles.summary: 欧洲航天器观测DART小行星撞击实验后的混乱现场，发现撞击造成的碎片分布远超预期。

articles.title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
articles.content: The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.
articles.summary: 隐私搜索服务Kagi推出Gmail竞品，结合隐私承诺与AI功能，挑战谷歌邮箱主导地位。

articles.title: Backblaze explains why it's sharing customer information with advertisers
articles.content: Backblaze tells Ars it won't share users' backup, storage files with advertisers.
articles.summary: Backblaze回应争议，称仅与广告商共享客户信息，不会分享用户的备份和存储文件。

articles.title: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites
articles.content: This constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
articles.summary: FCC授权SpaceX部署100万颗卫星，将使在轨卫星数量增加约50倍，引发轨道资源担忧。

articles.title: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
articles.content: An independent browser engine arrives on Linux and macOS, and we've tried it.
articles.summary: 独立浏览器引擎Ladybird发布首个可下载Alpha版，登陆Linux和macOS，功能表现超出预期。

articles.title: Etsy clarifies AI terms after seller backlash
articles.content: One veteran illustrator dismisses revisions as "sugar coating."
articles.summary: Etsy在卖家反对后澄清AI相关条款，但资深插画师批评修订只是粉饰，未解决核心问题。

articles.title: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop
articles.content: Militaries have many reasons to target data centers and the cloud in wartime.
articles.summary: Ars Live回顾指出，战时军方有诸多理由攻击数据中心和云设施，此类威胁不会停止。

articles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review
articles.content: Ankit Jain of Aviator told QCon San Francisco 2026 that line-by-line code review is already fading, since most review comments concern knowledge sharing rather than defects and over 75% of PRs merge without human review. He proposed six layers: argue, capture, codify, prove, debate, own. His team merges four times more PRs, with about 40% fewer reverts. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: Aviator的Ankit Jain在QCon指出逐行代码审查正被淘汰，超75%的PR无需人工审查即合并，并提出六层替代方案。

articles.title: Building a Production-Ready Culture and Skills Through SRE-based Training
articles.content: Training can act as a confidence engine, turning repeated behaviors into habits and culture. We can tailor training programs that equip developers and operators with the skills to run their services in line with the organization’s maturity and growth, and apply SRE principles to the training itself. By Ben Linders
articles.summary: InfoQ介绍如何通过基于SRE的培训打造生产就绪文化，将重复行为转化为习惯，并按组织成熟度定制培训。

articles.title: Presentation: Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell
articles.content: Rachel Shalom explains how Dell solved enterprise RAG retrieval failures on internal terminology by fine-tuning open-source embedding models. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge. By Rachel Shalom
articles.summary: Dell的Rachel Shalom分享如何微调开源嵌入模型解决企业RAG检索失败，涵盖难负样本准备与分布式训练。

articles.title: .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload
articles.content: Microsoft released .NET 11 with a .NET MAUI update focused on product quality. CoreCLR is now the default runtime on all platforms, and XAML gets incremental hot reload, implicit namespaces and faster resource dictionaries. The release also adds device test templates and passkey support, and raises the minimum Android and Apple platform versions. By Edin Kapić
articles.summary: .NET MAUI 11将CoreCLR设为全平台默认运行时，新增增量XAML热重载、设备测试模板和通行密钥支持。

articles.title: Mock Service Worker Releases v3.0 with ESM-Only Build, Socket-Based Interception and GraphQL Subs
articles.content: Mock Service Worker 3.0 is now ESM-only, requires Node.js 22 or later, and cuts package size from 416KB to 234KB. It adds GraphQL subscription support, protocol-specific entrypoints, and an experimental defineNetwork API. Node.js interception now works at the TCP and TLS level. Some users report test failures from newly intercepted OPTIONS preflight requests. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: Mock Service Worker 3.0改为纯ESM构建，包体积从416KB降至234KB，新增GraphQL订阅和TCP层拦截。

articles.title: Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance
articles.content: At Ignite 2026, Microsoft positioned Copilot as the operating system for work and extended agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender. Highlights include Cobalt 200 VMs, Azure HorizonDB, a continuous improvement loop in Foundry, Microsoft IQ, a standalone Azure AI Gateway, and Windows Server 2028. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: 微软Ignite 2026将Copilot定位为工作操作系统，并在Azure、Foundry等平台扩展智能体治理与成本控制。

articles.title: DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 Aims to Make Robots Safer, More Dexterous, and Faster Learners
articles.content: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a vision-language-action (VLA) model designed to improve robots' dexterity, reliability, and learning speed, while enabling safer operation in unstructured real-world environments. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: DeepMind发布Gemini Robotics 2.5视觉语言动作模型，提升机器人灵巧性、可靠性和学习速度。

articles.title: GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR after Three-Year Migration
articles.content: GitHub migrated github.com from styled-components to CSS Modules over three years, reporting a 55% cut in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation. Primer components were converted behind feature flags, and about 7,760 sx prop usages were migrated with codemods and Copilot agents. Commenters questioned user impact and hashed class names. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: GitHub历时三年将github.com从styled-components迁移至CSS Modules，服务端渲染提速55%，组件初始化快25%。

articles.title: DoorDash Scales Dispatch 10x While Maintaining 99.99% Peak Availability
articles.content: DoorDash has redesigned its real-time dispatch platform, replacing a monolithic optimization engine with a distributed architecture that separates coordination from computation. The new system delivers 10x higher throughput and more than 99.99% peak availability. It also supports hybrid machine learning inference and multi-agent reinforcement learning to dynamically optimize delivery assignments. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: DoorDash重构实时调度平台，以分布式架构替代单体优化引擎，吞吐量提升10倍，峰值可用性超99.99%。

articles.title: Vercel Launched Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks across Humans and Coding Agents
articles.content: Vercel's experimental Board is a headless message store where people and coding agents claim leased tasks, declare dependencies, and sync threads with Slack, GitHub, and Linear. By Daniel Dominguez
articles.summary: Vercel推出实验性Board，作为无头消息存储，让人与编码智能体认领任务、声明依赖并同步Slack等工具。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #544: AI is now the most-cited risk in the Fed's survey: 87%, up from 50%
articles.content: The Federal Reserve asked its market contacts what could shake the financial system, and 87% named AI, up from 50% in the spring. The same week, the FAA halted flights nationwide days after putting an AI tool in every regional control center, and says it is still looking at what happened. Nvidia's board has approached Arm's CEO about replacing Jensen Huang. Russian pranksters got three OpenAI national security staff on a video call. In the middle: Anthropic prices its IPO on Wednesday with $900.9 billion in compute commitments on its books.
articles.summary: 美联储调查显示87%市场联系人将AI列为最受关注金融风险，较春季的50%大幅上升。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #543: Google is the latest tech giant to chase TypeSafe's 8-week-old Jev
articles.content: This issue is about decision models, a new kind of AI model that does not write text. You give it an input and a fixed list of answers, and it returns the best answer with a probability, in milliseconds. TypeSafe AI released the first one, Jev, on September 15. On Wednesday Google released its own, after OpenAI and Microsoft did in October, and all three charge $0.10 or less per million input tokens and nothing for output. Shanghai AI Lab says its 4B model beat Jev on its tests, and Microsoft built its model on Alibaba's Qwen. Chatbots still score a little higher on the hardest decisions, at 15 times the cost. In the middle: on Vercel's gateway, decision models took one in four AI requests in October.
articles.summary: TypeSafe AI 发布决策模型 Jev 后，谷歌等科技巨头迅速跟进推出同类产品，决策模型赛道竞争升温。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: 美国多州选举中，支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人有望在多达15场州长竞选中获胜，AI基建争议进入政治议程。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 微软、Alphabet、亚马逊本周集中发布财报，市场关注AI投入回报，同时CoreWeave债务违约风险引发信贷市场担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: 企业应用数据显示，AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，AI代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 中期选举中AI生成或增强的广告支出超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI，监管透明度问题凸显。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能家电等家庭设备上，引发对AI扩散安全的担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶尖AI模型在自主开展AI研究的测试中失败，业界关注AI能否独立做科研及其治理与军事应用走向。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，同时大规模部署进入日常使用，部分场景开始限制或移除AI。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝Turnitin新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI正重塑大学评分体系。

articles.title: Warp bets on the software factory
articles.content: Zach Lloyd, founder and CEO of Warp, is back to talk about what he calls the company's primary bet: Warp Factories, open infrastructure for running a cloud software factory, which he calls the new version of CI/CD. He explains factory as code, what's inside an agent trace, why self-improving systems drift, and how his senior engineers went from guardians of the code to the biggest adopters once the models got good enough. Then he and Adam get into whether this is a pivot, why the best interface might be no new interface at all, coding as a team in Slack, and Adam's case for continuous flow.
articles.summary: Warp CEO介绍公司核心押注Warp Factories，称其为CI/CD新形态，提供运行云端软件工厂的开放基础设施。

articles.title: A seminal moment in computing
articles.content: MG, founder and CEO of WorkOS, is back to talk about leading a company through what DHH called a seminal moment in computing. He explains Atlas, the AI coworker WorkOS built for itself and then launched, why agents will soon choose and sign up for your tech stack, and why this moment feels closer to fire than to the iPhone. Then he gets practical: starting a company is easier than ever, but product-market fit is harder, so be a heat-seeking missile for pain, pick customers you like, and stop calling yourself non-technical.
articles.summary: WorkOS CEO谈公司自研并推出的AI同事Atlas，预测AI代理将自主选择并注册技术栈，标志计算进入新阶段。

articles.title: Orbin' with Amp
articles.content: Quinn Slack is back and we're talking about the next level for Amp. Agents write the code, they review the code, and they can push it to main (like our friends at Amp). But where should your agents live? Who remembers what you actually asked them to do? Amp is now its own company, and Quinn has a lot to say about orbs, threads that last forever, and why code review as we know it is fading. He explains why the model matters less than it used to, and why he worries we could lose the open source commons. Quinn even built a feature request live on the show to solve my tailnet problem.
articles.summary: Amp独立成公司，Quinn Slack介绍代理可编写、审查并推送代码，探讨代理应运行于何处及任务记忆问题。

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who's checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I'm joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet.
articles.summary: Socket CTO Ahmad Nassri 探讨 AI 代理自动选包安装带来的供应链信任风险，以及攻击者利用代理的新手法。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr 提出“Kerr 定律”，指出团队最大瓶颈是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建保持同步，尤其在审查代理代码时。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens 谈 Postgres 扩展生态、pg_lake 引入 DuckDB 与 Iceberg，以及 AI 对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 分享如何用 Go 重写支撑 300 万用户的邮件服务，并布局面向 AI 代理的产品。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen 将 40 小时周末项目 NanoClaw 打造成爆红开源项目，并基于容器隔离安全方案创立企业 AI 公司。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out.
